```tsx
  // cache with sync enabled.
  const [, setCache] = useCache<string>("cache-key", { cache: sharedCache });
  const [readerValue] = useCache<string>("cache-key", {
    cache: sharedCache,
    cacheSync: true,
    defaultValue: "default value",
  });

  return (
    <>
      <div>
        <button onClick={() => setCache(Math.random().toString())}>Set random value</button>{" "}
        <button onClick={() => setCache(undefined)}>Remove</button>
      </div>
      <div>The synced reader value is: {readerValue}</div>
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

### Persist to storage

`useCache` stores data in memory only. To make the cache survive page reloads, extend [`LRUCache`](https://github.com/isaacs/node-lru-cache) with a write-through subclass: `set` writes the value back to the storage, and the `dispose` hook removes the persisted copy whenever an entry leaves the in-memory cache (delete, eviction, expiry purge or overwrite). The subclass restores persisted entries in its constructor and stores an `expiresAt` timestamp per entry, so expired data is dropped on restore.

`StorageCache` persists to `localStorage` by default; pass `sessionStorage` via the `storage` option for a session-scoped cache. Because the persistence lives inside the cache subclass, every write is persisted automatically, including writes made directly through `cache.set` — no per-hook `onSet`/`onDelete` options are needed. The same instance can be shared with [`useLoad`](useLoad.md#persist-cached-data-to-storage) through its `cache` option.

```tsx
import { useCache } from "@lilib/hooks";

import StorageCache from "./StorageCache";

// Persist to localStorage by default, or pass another storage for a
// different scope: `new StorageCache({ storage: window.sessionStorage })`.
const cache = new StorageCache();
const CACHE_KEY = "cache-key";

function Example() {
  const [value, setCache] = useCache<string>(CACHE_KEY, {
    cache,
    cacheTime: cache.cacheTime,
    defaultValue: "default value",
  });

  return (
    <>
      <div>
        <button onClick={() => setCache(Math.random().toString())}>Set random value</button>{" "}
        <button onClick={() => setCache(undefined)}>Remove</button>
      </div>
      <div>The value is: {value}</div>
      <div>Reload the page — the value survives.</div>
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

**The full `StorageCache` implementation**

**StorageCache.ts**

```tsx
import { LRUCache } from "lru-cache";

export interface StorageCacheOptions {
  /** Storage to persist to. Defaults to `window.localStorage`. Pass `window.sessionStorage` for a session-scoped cache. */
  storage?: Storage | null;
  /** Key prefix in the storage. Default is `"lilib:"`. Pass a distinct prefix when multiple cache instances share the same storage. */
  prefix?: string;
  /** Cache time in milliseconds, used to compute the persisted TTL. Default is 5 minutes. */
  cacheTime?: number;
  /** Maximum number of in-memory entries. Default is `100`. */
  max?: number;
}

interface PersistedEntry {
  value: any;
  // `JSON.stringify` turns `Infinity` into `null`, so `null` is read back as
  // `Infinity` (a permanent cache) instead of `NaN`.
  expiresAt: number | null;
}

// A write-through `LRUCache` that persists its entries to a `Storage`
// (`localStorage` by default, or `sessionStorage` via the `storage` option),
// so the cache survives page reloads. `set` writes the value to the storage,
// and `dispose` removes the persisted copy whenever an entry leaves the
// in-memory cache (delete, eviction, expiry purge or overwrite). Persisted
// entries are restored synchronously in the constructor. Share an instance
// between `useCache` and `useLoad` through their `cache` option.
export class StorageCache extends LRUCache<string, any> {
  /** The cache time used to compute the persisted TTL. Pass it to the `cacheTime` options of `useCache`/`useLoad`. */
  readonly cacheTime: number;

  private storage: Storage | null;
  private prefix: string;

  constructor(options: StorageCacheOptions = {}) {
    const { storage, prefix = "lilib:", cacheTime = 5 * 60 * 1000, max = 100 } = options;
    super({
      max,
      dispose: (_value, key) => this.removePersistedEntry(key),
    });
    this.storage = storage ?? StorageCache.getDefaultStorage();
    this.prefix = prefix;
    this.cacheTime = cacheTime;
    // Storage reads are synchronous, so persisted entries can be restored
    // right in the constructor — no loading state is needed.
    if (this.storage) {
      this.hydrate();
    }
  }

  // Accessing `window.localStorage` can throw (blocked storage, private
  // browsing) — fall back to a disabled cache instead of crashing.
  private static getDefaultStorage(): Storage | null {
    if (typeof window === "undefined") {
      return null;
    }
    try {
      return window.localStorage;
    } catch {
      return null;
    }
  }

  override set(key: string, value: any, options?: LRUCache.SetOptions<string, any, unknown>): this {
    const result = super.set(key, value, options);
    // `LRUCache` treats `set(key, undefined)` as `delete(key)` — nothing to persist.
    if (value !== undefined) {
      // Write through. Overwrites dispose the old entry first, so the old
      // persisted copy is removed before the new one is written.
      this.writePersistedEntry(
        key,
        value,
        StorageCache.toExpiresAt(options?.ttl ?? this.cacheTime),
      );
    }
    return result;
  }

  // `LRUCache` treats `ttl: 0` and `ttl: Infinity` as "never expires"
  // (`useLoad` maps an infinite `cacheTime` to `ttl: 0`), so both mean a
  // permanent entry.
  private static toExpiresAt(ttl: number) {
    return ttl > 0 && ttl < Infinity ? Date.now() + ttl : Infinity;
  }

  // Restore persisted entries, dropping expired ones. Iterate backwards:
  // removing an expired entry shifts the storage indices, and entries behind
  // the cursor have already been visited.
  private hydrate() {
    const storage = this.storage;
    if (!storage) {
      return;
    }
    // Storage access can throw (blocked storage, private browsing) — treat
    // it as an empty cache.
    try {
      for (let i = storage.length - 1; i >= 0; i -= 1) {
        const storageKey = storage.key(i);
        if (storageKey && storageKey.startsWith(this.prefix)) {
          const key = storageKey.slice(this.prefix.length);
          const entry = this.readPersistedEntry(key);
          const ttl = (entry?.expiresAt == null ? Infinity : entry.expiresAt) - Date.now();
          if (entry && ttl > 0) {
            // `super.set` restores the entry without persisting it again.
            super.set(key, entry.value, { ttl });
          } else {
            this.removePersistedEntry(key);
          }
        }
      }
    } catch {
      // The in-memory cache stays empty.
    }
  }

  private readPersistedEntry(key: string): PersistedEntry | undefined {
    try {
      const raw = this.storage?.getItem(this.prefix + key);
      if (raw == null) {
        return undefined;
      }
      return JSON.parse(raw) as PersistedEntry;
    } catch {
      return undefined;
    }
  }

  private writePersistedEntry(key: string, value: any, expiresAt: number) {
    // Persisting is best-effort: quota errors or non-serializable values
    // must not break the caller — the in-memory cache remains the source
    // of truth.
    try {
      this.storage?.setItem(this.prefix + key, JSON.stringify({ value, expiresAt }));
    } catch {
      // Ignore.
    }
  }

  private removePersistedEntry(key: string) {
    try {
      this.storage?.removeItem(this.prefix + key);
    } catch {
      // Ignore.
    }
  }
}

export default StorageCache;
```

### Persist to IndexedDB

IndexedDB is asynchronous, so `IndexedDBCache` cannot restore persisted entries in its constructor: call `hydrate` in an effect after mount, and render the `useCache` call only after hydration finishes. `useCache` reads the cache exactly once on its first render, so calling it before hydration would permanently miss the persisted value. The write-through layer is the same as in `StorageCache`, except that the IndexedDB operations are async and fire-and-forget. The same instance can be shared with [`useLoad`](useLoad.md#persist-cached-data-to-indexeddb) through its `cache` option.

```tsx
import { useCache, useMount, useSafeState } from "@lilib/hooks";

import IndexedDBCache from "./IndexedDBCache";

const cache = new IndexedDBCache();
const CACHE_KEY = "cache-key";

function CachedValue() {
  const [value, setCache] = useCache<string>(CACHE_KEY, {
    cache,
    cacheTime: cache.cacheTime,
    defaultValue: "default value",
  });

  return (
    <>
      <div>
        <button onClick={() => setCache(Math.random().toString())}>Set random value</button>{" "}
        <button onClick={() => setCache(undefined)}>Remove</button>
      </div>
      <div>The value is: {value}</div>
      <div>Reload the page — the value survives.</div>
    </>
  );
}

function Example() {
  const [hydrated, setHydrated] = useSafeState(false);

  useMount(() => {
    cache
      .hydrate()
      .catch((error) => {
        // IndexedDB may be unavailable (private browsing, etc.) — proceed
        // with an empty cache instead of blocking forever.
        console.error(error);
      })
      .then(() => setHydrated(true));
  });

  if (!hydrated) {
    return <div>Loading persisted data…</div>;
  }

  return <CachedValue />;
}

export default Example;
```

**The full `IndexedDBCache` implementation**

**IndexedDBCache.ts**

```tsx
import { LRUCache } from "lru-cache";

export interface IndexedDBCacheOptions {
  /** Database name. Default is `"lilib"`. Pass a distinct name when multiple apps share the same origin. */
  databaseName?: string;
  /** Object store name. Default is `"hooks"`. */
  storeName?: string;
  /** Cache time in milliseconds, used to compute the persisted TTL. Default is 5 minutes. */
  cacheTime?: number;
  /** Maximum number of in-memory entries. Default is `100`. */
  max?: number;
}

interface PersistedEntry {
  value: any;
  expiresAt: number;
}

// A write-through `LRUCache` that persists its entries to IndexedDB, so the
// cache survives page reloads. Unlike `StorageCache`, IndexedDB is
// asynchronous, so the cache cannot be restored in the constructor: call
// `hydrate` before rendering any `useCache`/`useLoad` call that uses this
// instance. Share an instance between `useCache` and `useLoad` through their
// `cache` option.
export class IndexedDBCache extends LRUCache<string, any> {
  /** The cache time used to compute the persisted TTL. Pass it to the `cacheTime` options of `useCache`/`useLoad`. */
  readonly cacheTime: number;

  private databaseName: string;
  private storeName: string;
  private databasePromise: Promise<IDBDatabase> | undefined;

  constructor(options: IndexedDBCacheOptions = {}) {
    const {
      databaseName = "lilib",
      storeName = "hooks",
      cacheTime = 5 * 60 * 1000,
      max = 100,
    } = options;
    super({
      max,
      // Remove the persisted copy whenever an entry leaves the in-memory
      // cache (delete, eviction, expiry purge or overwrite). IndexedDB writes
      // are async, so the removals are fire-and-forget (failures are ignored)
      // — the in-memory cache remains the source of truth.
      dispose: (_value, key) => {
        void this.removeEntry(key).catch(() => {});
      },
    });
    this.databaseName = databaseName;
    this.storeName = storeName;
    this.cacheTime = cacheTime;
  }

  override set(key: string, value: any, options?: LRUCache.SetOptions<string, any, unknown>): this {
    const result = super.set(key, value, options);
    // `LRUCache` treats `set(key, undefined)` as `delete(key)` — nothing to persist.
    if (value !== undefined) {
      void this.writeEntry(key, {
        value,
        expiresAt: IndexedDBCache.toExpiresAt(options?.ttl ?? this.cacheTime),
      }).catch(() => {});
    }
    return result;
  }

  // `LRUCache` treats `ttl: 0` and `ttl: Infinity` as "never expires"
  // (`useLoad` maps an infinite `cacheTime` to `ttl: 0`), so both mean a
  // permanent entry.
  private static toExpiresAt(ttl: number) {
    return ttl > 0 && ttl < Infinity ? Date.now() + ttl : Infinity;
  }

  // Restore persisted entries into the cache, dropping expired ones. Skip
  // entries that a previous run (e.g. StrictMode's double invocation) has
  // already restored: overwriting them would dispose and delete the persisted
  // copy.
  async hydrate() {
    const entries = await this.readAllEntries();
    for (const [key, entry] of entries) {
      if (this.has(key)) {
        continue;
      }
      const ttl = entry.expiresAt - Date.now();
      if (ttl > 0) {
        // `super.set` restores the entry without persisting it again.
        super.set(key, entry.value, { ttl });
      } else {
        void this.removeEntry(key).catch(() => {});
      }
    }
  }

  // One lazy connection for all operations. IndexedDB serializes transactions
  // on a connection, so operations run in the order they are created.
  private getDatabase(): Promise<IDBDatabase> {
    if (!this.databasePromise) {
      this.databasePromise = this.openDatabase()
        .then((db) => {
          if (db.objectStoreNames.contains(this.storeName)) {
            return db;
          }
          // The database exists but the store is missing (e.g. it was created
          // by an older build with a different store name, so no upgrade ever
          // ran): close it and reopen with a bumped version so
          // `onupgradeneeded` fires and creates the store.
          const nextVersion = db.version + 1;
          db.close();
          return this.openDatabase(nextVersion);
        })
        .catch((error) => {
          // A transient failure (e.g. the version upgrade is blocked by an
          // open connection) must not disable persistence forever — allow
          // the next operation to retry.
          this.databasePromise = undefined;
          throw error;
        });
    }
    return this.databasePromise;
  }

  private openDatabase(version?: number): Promise<IDBDatabase> {
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      const request = indexedDB.open(this.databaseName, version);
      request.onupgradeneeded = () => {
        if (!request.result.objectStoreNames.contains(this.storeName)) {
          request.result.createObjectStore(this.storeName);
        }
      };
      request.onsuccess = () => resolve(request.result);
      request.onerror = () => reject(request.error);
      request.onblocked = () => {
        reject(
          new Error(
            `Upgrading the "${this.databaseName}" database is blocked by another connection.`,
          ),
        );
      };
    });
  }

  private async readAllEntries(): Promise<Array<[string, PersistedEntry]>> {
    const db = await this.getDatabase();
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      const request = db
        .transaction(this.storeName, "readonly")
        .objectStore(this.storeName)
        .openCursor();
      const entries: Array<[string, PersistedEntry]> = [];
      request.onsuccess = () => {
        const cursor = request.result;
        if (cursor) {
          entries.push([cursor.key as string, cursor.value as PersistedEntry]);
          cursor.continue();
        } else {
          resolve(entries);
        }
      };
      request.onerror = () => reject(request.error);
    });
  }

  private async writeEntry(key: string, entry: PersistedEntry): Promise<void> {
    const db = await this.getDatabase();
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      const request = db
        .transaction(this.storeName, "readwrite")
        .objectStore(this.storeName)
        .put(entry, key);
      request.onsuccess = () => resolve();
      request.onerror = () => reject(request.error);
    });
  }

  private async removeEntry(key: string): Promise<void> {
    const db = await this.getDatabase();
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      const request = db
        .transaction(this.storeName, "readwrite")
        .objectStore(this.storeName)
        .delete(key);
      request.onsuccess = () => resolve();
      request.onerror = () => reject(request.error);
    });
  }
}

export default IndexedDBCache;
```

---

# useToggle

Manage a boolean value.

## API

```ts
function useToggle(initialValue?: boolean): [
  value: boolean,
  actions: {
    toggle: (newValue?: boolean) => void;
    toggleOn: () => void;
    toggleOff: () => void;
  },
];
```

Parameters:

- **`initialValue`:** Optional initial value. Default is `false`.

Results:

- **`value`:** A boolean value that can be changed by the following actions.
- **`actions`:** Actions object.
  - **`actions.toggle`:** Toggle the `value`. If the `newValue` param is not `undefined`, the `value` will be set to `newValue` (cast to boolean).
  - **`actions.toggleOn`:** Set the `value` to `true`.
  - **`actions.toggleOff`:** Set the `value` to `false`.

## Example

The following example controls a details panel with the toggle actions.

```tsx
import { useToggle } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const [on, { toggle, toggleOn, toggleOff }] = useToggle(true);

  return (
    <>
      <div>
        <button onClick={() => toggle()}>Toggle</button> <button onClick={toggleOn}>Turn on</button>{" "}
        <button onClick={toggleOff}>Turn off</button>
      </div>
      <div>The switch is {on ? "on" : "off"}</div>
      {on && (
        <div style={{ padding: 8, marginTop: 8, backgroundColor: "rgba(255, 165, 0, 0.3)" }}>
          Details panel
        </div>
      )}
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

---

# useSetState

This hook is like the `this.setState` method of class components. It requires an object as the initial state, and can update part of the state. The new state will be merged with the old state.

## API

```ts
function useSetState<S extends object>(
  initialState: S | (() => S),
): [state: S, setState: (patch: Partial<S> | ((prevState: S) => Partial<S>)) => void];
```

Parameters:

- **`initialState`:** The initial state object, or a function that returns it.

Results:

- **`state`:** The current state object.
- **`setState`:** Update part of the state; the patch will be merged with the old state. The `patch` can be an object or a function computed from the previous state.

## Notes

- Merging is shallow: patching a nested object replaces the whole nested value. Use the functional form with a manual spread to merge deeply.

## Example

The following example manages a form's fields in one state object, updating one field at a time.

```tsx
import { useSetState } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const [state, setState] = useSetState({ firstName: "", lastName: "" });

  return (
    <>
      <p>
        First name:{" "}
        <input
          value={state.firstName}
          onChange={(event) => {
            setState({ firstName: event.target.value });
          }}
        />
      </p>
      <p>
        Last name:{" "}
        <input
          value={state.lastName}
          onChange={(event) => {
            setState({ lastName: event.target.value });
          }}
        />
      </p>
      <div>
        Full name: {state.firstName} {state.lastName}
      </div>
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

---

# useSafeState

This hook is used in the same way as `React.useState`, except that calling `setState` after the component is unmounted has no effect rather than throwing an error.

## API

```ts
function useSafeState<S>(
  initialState: S | (() => S),
): [state: S, setState: React.Dispatch<React.SetStateAction<S>>];

function useSafeState<S = undefined>(): [
  state: S | undefined,
  setState: React.Dispatch<React.SetStateAction<S | undefined>>,
];
```

Parameters:

- **`initialState`:** The initial state, same as `React.useState`. It can be a value or a function that returns the value.

Results:

- **`state`:** The current state.
- **`setState`:** Update the state. Calling it after the component unmounts has no effect and never errors.

## Example

A typical use: fetch data asynchronously and call `setState` after the request finishes; it is safe even if the component unmounts in the meantime.

```tsx
import { useMount, useSafeState } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const [data, setData] = useSafeState<any>();

  useMount(async () => {
    const response = await fetch("http://example.com/api/getData");
    setData(await response.json());
  });

  ...
}
```

---

# useControllableState

Unify a value that can be either controlled or uncontrolled, which is the common requirement of form and overlay components.

## API

```ts
interface UseControllableStateOptions<T> {
  value?: T;
  defaultValue?: T;
  onChange?: (value: T) => void;
}

function useControllableState<T>(
  options: UseControllableStateOptions<T> & { defaultValue: T },
): [state: T, setState: (nextState: T | ((prevState: T) => T)) => void];

function useControllableState<T>(
  options: UseControllableStateOptions<T> & { value: T },
): [state: T, setState: (nextState: T | ((prevState: T) => T)) => void];

function useControllableState<T>(
  options?: UseControllableStateOptions<T>,
): [
  state: T | undefined,
  setState: (nextState: T | undefined | ((prevState: T | undefined) => T | undefined)) => void,
];
```

Parameters:

- **`options`:** Options object.
  - **`options.value`:** The controlled value. The state is controlled whenever `value` is not `undefined`. Keep it defined for the whole lifetime of the component; falling back to `undefined` turns the state into uncontrolled.
  - **`options.defaultValue`:** The initial value used while the state is uncontrolled. It is ignored when `value` is provided, and later changes to it do not reset the state.
  - **`options.onChange`:** Called with the next value once it actually changes, in both controlled and uncontrolled modes.

Results:

- **`state`:** The current value: `value` when controlled, the internal state otherwise.
- **`setState`:** Accepts a new value or an updater function computed from the current value. It calls `onChange` only when the value actually changes and keeps a stable identity.

## Notes

- A controlled component must update `value` in `onChange`; otherwise the state never changes, because `setState` does not touch the internal state while controlled.
- `value` is compared with the previous one using `Object.is`, so setting an unchanged value does not call `onChange`.
- Switching between controlled and uncontrolled is supported: the state resumes from the latest value of the previous mode, starting with the very first render after the switch. Prefer keeping a component in one mode for its whole lifetime.
- `undefined` always means uncontrolled, so it cannot be a controlled value. Use a sentinel such as `null` when a controlled value has to represent "empty".
- To get `state: T` instead of `T | undefined`, make `defaultValue` non-optional in the type, for example by destructuring it with a default (`{ value, defaultValue = "" }`). Otherwise the last overload is selected and `undefined` is included in the result type.

## Example

The following example renders the same field component in both controlled and uncontrolled modes: the controlled field follows the parent state, while the uncontrolled one keeps its own state.

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";

import { useControllableState } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Field({
  value,
  defaultValue = "",
  onChange,
}: {
  value?: string;
  defaultValue?: string;
  onChange?: (value: string) => void;
}) {
  const [text, setText] = useControllableState({ value, defaultValue, onChange });

  return <input value={text} onChange={(event) => setText(event.target.value)} />;
}

function Example() {
  const [value, setValue] = useState("Controlled value");

  return (
    <>
      <div>
        Controlled: <Field value={value} onChange={setValue} />{" "}
        <button onClick={() => setValue("Reset from outside")}>Reset</button>
      </div>
      <div style={{ marginTop: 8 }}>
        Uncontrolled: <Field defaultValue="Initial value" />
      </div>
      <div style={{ marginTop: 8 }}>Controlled value: {value}</div>
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

---

# useDelayedValue

Delay updates to a value.

## API

```ts
function useDelayedValue<T>(
  value: T,
  options:
    | number
    | {
        delay: number;
        shouldDelay?: (value: any) => boolean;
        compare?: (x: any, y: any) => boolean;
      },
): T;
```

Parameters:

- **`value`:** The value whose updates will be delayed.
- **`options`:** The delay time (milliseconds) or an options object.
  - **`options.delay`:** Delay time, in milliseconds. It must be a positive number.
  - **`options.shouldDelay`:** A function that determines whether an update should be delayed. Returning `false` updates immediately and synchronously. Any value is delayed by default.
  - **`options.compare`:** A function to determine whether the new and old values are equal, defaults to `Object.is`.

Results:

- Returns the delayed value.

## Notes

- The initial render returns `value` immediately; only subsequent updates are delayed.
- `shouldDelay` returning `false` applies the update immediately and synchronously.
- The default `compare` is `Object.is`: a new object each render triggers an update every time.

## Example

In the following example, showing `"Loading..."` is delayed for 500ms after the value changes to `true`; changes to `false` are applied immediately.

```tsx
import { useDelayedValue, useToggle } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const [loading, { toggle }] = useToggle(false);
  const delayedLoading = useDelayedValue(loading, {
    delay: 500,
    shouldDelay: (value) => value === true,
  });

  return (
    <div>
      <button onClick={() => toggle()}>Toggle</button>
      {delayedLoading && "Loading..."}
    </div>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

---

# useMemoizedValue

Return the previous value when the value has not changed. Use deep comparison by default.

## API

```ts
function useMemoizedValue<T>(value: T, compare?: (x: any, y: any) => boolean): T;
```

Parameters:

- **`value`:** The value.
- **`compare`:** A function to determine whether the new and old values are equal, defaults to deep comparison.

Results:

- Returns the previous value if unchanged, otherwise the current value.

## Notes

- The default comparison is a deep comparison, which can be costly for large values; pass a custom `compare` for cheap cases.
- The first render always returns the initial value.

## Example

A typical use: building a `useMemo` with deep-compared dependencies.

```ts
import { useMemo, DependencyList } from "react";
import { useMemoizedValue } from "@lilib/hooks";

function useDeepCompareMemo<T>(factory: () => T, deps?: DependencyList): T {
  return useMemo(factory, useMemoizedValue(deps));
}

export default useDeepCompareMemo;
```

---

# useThrottledValue

Throttle a value.

## API

```ts
function useThrottledValue<T>(
  value: T,
  options?: number | { wait?: number; leading?: boolean; trailing?: boolean },
): [
  throttledValue: T,
  actions: {
    flush: (finalValue?: T) => void;
    cancel: () => void;
  },
];
```

Parameters:

- **`value`:** The value to throttle.
- **`options`:** Throttle wait time or an options object.
  - **`options.wait`:** Throttle wait time, in milliseconds. Default is `0`.
  - **`options.leading`:** Change throttled value on the leading edge. Default is `false`.
  - **`options.trailing`:** Change throttled value on the trailing edge. Default is `true`.

Results:

- **`throttledValue`:** Throttled value.
- **`actions`:** Actions object.
  - **`actions.flush`:** Flush function. The `finalValue` will be returned as `throttledValue` if it is specified.
  - **`actions.cancel`:** Cancel throttle timer.

## Notes

- The initial render returns `value` immediately; only subsequent changes are throttled.
- With the default `leading: false`, updates land on the trailing edge only.
- The pending update is cancelled on unmount.

## Example

The following example shows a search box; requests are only sent when the throttled value changes.

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { useThrottledValue, useUpdate } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const [value, setValue] = useState("");
  const [throttledValue] = useThrottledValue(value, 500);
  const [requests, setRequests] = useState(0);

  // Simulate a search request whenever the throttled value changes.
  useUpdate(() => {
    setRequests((requests) => requests + 1);
  }, [throttledValue]);

  return (
    <>
      <p>
        Enter search keywords:{" "}
        <input
          value={value}
          onChange={(event) => {
            setValue(event.target.value);
          }}
        />
      </p>
      <div>Throttled keywords: {throttledValue || "—"}</div>
      <div>Search requests sent: {requests}</div>
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

---

# useDebouncedValue

Debounce a value.

## API

```ts
function useDebouncedValue<T>(
  value: T,
  options?: number | { wait?: number; maxWait?: number; leading?: boolean; trailing?: boolean },
): [
  debouncedValue: T,
  actions: {
    flush: (finalValue?: T) => void;
    cancel: () => void;
  },
];
```

Parameters:

- **`value`:** The value to debounce.
- **`options`:** Debounce wait time or an options object.
  - **`options.wait`:** Debounce wait time, in milliseconds. Default is `0`.
  - **`options.maxWait`:** Max wait time, in milliseconds. Default is `Infinity`.
  - **`options.leading`:** Change debounced value on the leading edge. Default is `false`.
  - **`options.trailing`:** Change debounced value on the trailing edge. Default is `true`.

Results:

- **`debouncedValue`:** Debounced value.
- **`actions`:** Actions object.
  - **`actions.flush`:** Flush function. The `finalValue` will be returned as `debouncedValue` if it is specified.
  - **`actions.cancel`:** Cancel debounce timer.

## Notes

- The initial render returns `value` immediately; only subsequent changes are debounced.
- The pending update is cancelled on unmount.

## Example

The following example shows a search box; requests are only sent when the debounced value changes.

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { useDebouncedValue, useUpdate } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const [value, setValue] = useState("");

  const [requests, setRequests] = useState(0);

  // Simulate a search request whenever the debounced value changes.
  useUpdate(() => {
    setRequests((requests) => requests + 1);
  }, [debouncedValue]);

  return (
    <>
      <p>
        Enter search keywords:{" "}
        <input
          value={value}
          onChange={(event) => {
            setValue(event.target.value);
          }}
        />
      </p>
      <div>Debounced keywords: {debouncedValue || "—"}</div>
      <div>Search requests sent: {requests}</div>
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

# useRaf

Use [requestAnimationFrame](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/window/requestAnimationFrame) to invoke the callback before the browser repaints.

## API

```ts
function useRaf(callback: () => void): [start: () => void, cancel: () => void];
```

Parameters:

- **`callback`:** The callback invoked before the browser repaints.

Results:

- **`start`:** Starts the animation frame.
- **`cancel`:** Cancels the animation frame.

## Notes

- Calling `start` again cancels the previous animation frame.
- The pending callback is cancelled on unmount.

## Example

The following example animates a progress bar with requestAnimationFrame.

```tsx
import { useRef, useState } from "react";
import { useRaf } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const [progress, setProgress] = useState(0);
  const startTimeRef = useRef(0);
  const loopRef = useRef<() => void>(() => {});

  const [start, cancel] = useRaf(() => {
    if (!startTimeRef.current) {
      startTimeRef.current = Date.now();
    }
    const elapsed = Date.now() - startTimeRef.current;
    setProgress(Math.min(elapsed / 2000, 1));
    if (elapsed < 2000) {
      // Re-schedule until the animation completes.
      loopRef.current();
    }
  });

  loopRef.current = start;

  function handleStart() {
    startTimeRef.current = 0;
    setProgress(0);
    start();
  }

  return (
    <>
      <div>
        <button onClick={handleStart}>Start</button> <button onClick={cancel}>Cancel</button>
      </div>
      <div style={{ height: 8, marginTop: 8, backgroundColor: "rgba(128, 128, 128, 0.2)" }}>
        <div
          style={{ width: progress * 100 + "%", height: "100%", backgroundColor: "orange" }}
        ></div>
      </div>
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

---

# useIdle

Invoke the callback when the browser is idle. This hook uses [window.requestIdleCallback](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/requestIdleCallback) by default. If `window.requestIdleCallback` is unavailable, it falls back to `setTimeout`.

## API

```ts
function useIdle(
  callback: () => void,
  options?: IdleRequestOptions,
): [start: () => void, cancel: () => void];
```

Parameters:

- **`callback`:** The callback invoked when idle.
- **`options`:** The options passed to [window.requestIdleCallback](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/requestIdleCallback).

Results:

- **`start`:** Starts the idle callback.
- **`cancel`:** Cancels the idle callback.

## Notes

- Calling `start` again cancels the previous idle callback.
- The pending callback is cancelled on unmount.

## Example

The following example runs a low-priority task (e.g. analytics) when the browser is idle.

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { useIdle } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const [logs, setLogs] = useState<string[]>([]);
  const [start, cancel] = useIdle(() => {
    setLogs((logs) => [...logs, `Idle task done at ${new Date().toLocaleTimeString()}`]);
  });

  return (
    <>
      <div>
        <button onClick={start}>Start idle task</button> <button onClick={cancel}>Cancel</button>
      </div>
      <ul style={{ margin: 0, paddingLeft: 24 }}>
        {logs.map((log, index) => (
          <li key={index}>{log}</li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

---

# useAnimate

Run JavaScript animations with this hook.

## API

```ts
function useAnimate(
  callback: (percent: number) => void,
  options: number | { duration: number; algorithm?: (percent: number) => number },
): [start: () => void, cancel: () => void];
```

Parameters:

- **`callback`:** The animation step function. It receives a percent number between 0 and 1 as the first param.
- **`options`:** The animation duration (milliseconds), or an options object.
  - **`options.duration`:** The duration in milliseconds. Required in the options-object form; ignored when a number is passed directly.
  - **`options.algorithm`:** Optional easing function. The animation runs linearly by default, use this option to override the default behavior.

Results:

- **`start`:** Starts the animation.
- **`cancel`:** Cancels the animation.

## Notes

- The `duration` option must be a positive number; a warning is emitted otherwise.
- `start` cancels a running animation and restarts it from the beginning.
- `algorithm` receives the linear percent and should map it back to the `[0, 1]` range.

## Example

The following example animates a progress bar with a TweenJS easing function.

```tsx
import { useRef } from "react";
import TweenJS from "@tweenjs/tween.js";
import { useAnimate } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const domRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const [start, cancel] = useAnimate(
    (percent) => {
      if (domRef.current) {
        domRef.current.style.width = percent * 100 + "%";
      }
    },
    {
      duration: 1000,
      algorithm: TweenJS.Easing.Bounce.Out,
    },
  );

  return (
    <>
      <div>
        <button onClick={start}>Start</button> <button onClick={cancel}>Cancel</button>
      </div>
      <div
        ref={domRef}
        style={{ width: 0, height: 8, marginTop: 8, backgroundColor: "orange" }}
      ></div>
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

---

# useTimeout

Execute a callback after a delay.

## API

```ts
function useTimeout(
  callback: () => void,
  timeout?: number,
): [start: () => void, cancel: () => void];
```

Parameters:

- **`callback`:** The callback to execute after the delay.
- **`timeout`:** Optional delay time, in milliseconds.

Results:

- **`start`:** Starts the timer. It clears any previous timer first.
- **`cancel`:** Cancels the timer.

## Notes

- The timer starts only when `start` is called.
- Calling `start` again resets the timer.
- The timer is cancelled on unmount.

## Example

The following example shows a toast message that disappears automatically after a delay.

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { useTimeout } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false);
  const [start, cancel] = useTimeout(() => {
    setShow(false);
  }, 1500);

  function handleShow() {
    setShow(true);
    start();
  }

  function handleCancel() {
    cancel();
    setShow(false);
  }

  return (
    <>
      <div>
        <button onClick={handleShow}>Show toast</button>{" "}
        <button onClick={handleCancel}>Cancel</button>
      </div>
      {show && (
        <div style={{ padding: 8, marginTop: 8, backgroundColor: "rgba(255, 165, 0, 0.3)" }}>
          A toast message
        </div>
      )}
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

---

# useInterval

Run a callback repeatedly at a fixed interval.

## API

```ts
function useInterval(
  callback: () => void,
  interval?: number,
): [start: () => void, cancel: () => void];
```

Parameters:

- **`callback`:** A function to be called at intervals.
- **`interval`:** The interval, in milliseconds.

Results:

- **`start`:** Starts the loop. It clears any previous loop first.
- **`cancel`:** Cancels the loop.

## Notes

- The loop is cancelled on unmount.

## Example

The following example shows an elapsed-seconds clock that starts automatically on mount.

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { useInterval, useMount } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const [elapsed, setElapsed] = useState(0);
  const [start, cancel] = useInterval(() => {
    setElapsed((elapsed) => elapsed + 1);
  }, 1000);

  // Start the clock automatically on mount.
  useMount(start);

  return (
    <>
      <div>
        <button onClick={cancel}>Pause</button> <button onClick={start}>Resume</button>
      </div>
      <div>Elapsed seconds: {elapsed}</div>
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

---

# usePersist

Return the same function identity regardless of how the `callback` argument changes. The returned function behaves exactly like `callback`. A typical use case: the callback must go into a dependency array (e.g. `useEffect`), yet calls should always use the latest logic.

## API

```ts
function usePersist<T extends (...args: any[]) => any>(
  callback: T,
): (...args: Parameters<T>) => ReturnType<T>;
```

Parameters:

- **`callback`:** The callback function.

## Example

The following example binds a document click listener only once, and it always reads the latest input value.

```tsx
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";
import { usePersist } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const [value, setValue] = useState("");
  const [lastSeen, setLastSeen] = useState("");

  // The callback identity never changes, so the listener is bound only once.
  const onClick = usePersist(() => {
    // Always reads the latest `value` (no stale closure).
    setLastSeen(value);
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    document.addEventListener("click", onClick);
    return () => {
      document.removeEventListener("click", onClick);
    };
  }, [onClick]);

  return (
    <>
      <p>
        Enter value:{" "}
        <input
          value={value}
          onChange={(event) => {
            setValue(event.target.value);
          }}
        />
      </p>
      <div>Last value read on click: {lastSeen || "—"}</div>
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

---

# useRerender

This hook returns a function that you can use to re-render the component. It is usually used to re-render mutable data.

## API

```ts
function useRerender(): () => void;
```

## Notes

- This is an escape hatch for mutable data; prefer state for values that affect rendering.
- Do not call it during render.

## Example

The following example updates a mutable value outside React state and re-renders to display it.

```tsx
import { useRef } from "react";
import { useRerender } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  // A mutable value that lives outside React state.
  const countRef = useRef(0);
  const rerender = useRerender();

  function handleClick() {
    countRef.current++;
    rerender();
  }

  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={handleClick}>+1</button> {countRef.current}
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

---

# useThrottle

Use a throttled callback.

## API

```ts
function useThrottle<T extends (...args: any[]) => any>(
  callback: T,
  options?: number | { wait?: number; leading?: boolean; trailing?: boolean },
): [
  throttledCallback: (...args: Parameters<T>) => ReturnType<T> | undefined,
  actions: {
    flush: () => ReturnType<T> | undefined;
    cancel: () => void;
  },
];
```

Parameters:

- **`callback`:** Original callback function.
- **`options`:** Throttle wait time or an options object.
  - **`options.wait`:** Throttle wait time, in milliseconds. Default is `0`.
  - **`options.leading`:** Run callback on the leading edge. Default is `false`.
  - **`options.trailing`:** Run callback on the trailing edge. Default is `true`.

Results:

- **`throttledCallback`:** Throttled callback.
- **`actions`:** Actions object.
  - **`actions.flush`:** Flush function. Run callback immediately.
  - **`actions.cancel`:** Cancel throttle timer.

## Notes

- The pending trailing invocation is cancelled on unmount — it never runs.
- With the default `leading: false`, the first call is delayed until the wait elapses.
- Changing the options mid-flight immediately flushes the pending invocation of the old throttled function.
- The returned function returns `undefined` when the invocation is deferred.

## Example

The following example shows how many times the callback actually runs after clicking the button rapidly.

```tsx
import { useRef, useState } from "react";
import { useThrottle } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const callsRef = useRef(0);
  const [runs, setRuns] = useState(0);

  const [throttledCall] = useThrottle(
    () => {
      callsRef.current++;
      setRuns(callsRef.current);
    },
    { wait: 500 },
  );

  return (
    <>
      <div>
        <button onClick={() => throttledCall()}>Throttled call</button>
      </div>
      <div>Callback actually runs: {runs}</div>
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

---

# useDebounce

Use a debounced callback.

## API

```ts
function useDebounce<T extends (...args: any[]) => any>(
  callback: T,
  options?: number | { wait?: number; maxWait?: number; leading?: boolean; trailing?: boolean },
): [
  debouncedCallback: (...args: Parameters<T>) => ReturnType<T> | undefined,
  actions: {
    flush: () => ReturnType<T> | undefined;
    cancel: () => void;
  },
];
```

Parameters:

- **`callback`:** Original callback function.
- **`options`:** Debounce wait time or an options object.
  - **`options.wait`:** Debounce wait time, in milliseconds. Default is `0`.
  - **`options.maxWait`:** Max wait time, in milliseconds. Default is `Infinity`.
  - **`options.leading`:** Run callback on the leading edge. Default is `false`.
  - **`options.trailing`:** Run callback on the trailing edge. Default is `true`.

Results:

- **`debouncedCallback`:** Debounced callback.
- **`actions`:** Actions object.
  - **`actions.flush`:** Flush function. Run callback immediately.
  - **`actions.cancel`:** Cancel debounce timer.

## Notes

- The pending trailing invocation is cancelled on unmount — it never runs.
- Changing the options mid-flight immediately flushes the pending invocation of the old debounced function.
- The returned function returns `undefined` when the invocation is deferred.
- With `leading: false` and `trailing: false`, the callback never runs.

## Example

The following example shows how many times the callback actually runs after clicking the button rapidly.

```tsx
import { useRef, useState } from "react";
import { useDebounce } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const callsRef = useRef(0);
  const [runs, setRuns] = useState(0);

  const [debouncedCall] = useDebounce(
    () => {
      callsRef.current++;
      setRuns(callsRef.current);
    },
    { wait: 500 },
  );

  return (
    <>
      <div>
        <button onClick={() => debouncedCall()}>Debounced call</button>
      </div>
      <div>Callback actually runs: {runs}</div>
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

---

# useLatestRef

Return a ref object whose `.current` property always points to the latest value. It is typically used to read the latest value inside long-lived callbacks (timers, event listeners) to avoid stale closures.

## API

```ts
function useLatestRef<T>(value: T): React.MutableRefObject<T>;
```

## Notes

- The ref is written during render and does not trigger re-renders; use state for reactive values.

## Example

The following example shows an interval that always reads the latest input value.

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { useInterval, useLatestRef } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const [value, setValue] = useState("");
  const [snapshot, setSnapshot] = useState("");
  const valueRef = useLatestRef(value);

  const [start, cancel] = useInterval(() => {
    // The interval callback is bound once, but reads the latest value via the ref.
    setSnapshot(valueRef.current);
  }, 1000);

  return (
    <>
      <p>
        Enter value:{" "}
        <input
          value={value}
          onChange={(event) => {
            setValue(event.target.value);
          }}
        />
      </p>
      <div>
        <button onClick={start}>Start</button> <button onClick={cancel}>Cancel</button>
      </div>
      <div>Interval snapshot: {snapshot || "—"}</div>
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

---

# usePreviousRef

Return a ref object whose `.current` property points to the value from the previous update, and is kept while the value is unchanged. The first time is `undefined`.

## API

```ts
function usePreviousRef<T>(value: T): React.MutableRefObject<T | undefined>;
```

## Notes

- Comparison is by reference (`!==`): an object with a new identity counts as changed even if its content is equal. Use a deep-comparing hook such as `useMemoizedValue` when needed.

## Example

The following example shows the value of the previous render.

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { usePreviousRef } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  const previousRef = usePreviousRef(count);

  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={() => setCount((count) => count + 1)}>+1</button>
      <div>Current: {count}</div>
      <div>Previous: {previousRef.current ?? "—"}</div>
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

---

# useComposedRef

This hook composes multiple refs into one. Ref objects, ref callbacks, `null` and `undefined` are all accepted, which makes it very useful when developing components.

## API

```ts
function useComposedRef<T>(...refs: (React.Ref<T> | undefined)[]): React.RefCallback<T>;
```

## Notes

- The returned callback keeps the same identity while the input refs remain unchanged.
- In React 19+, detachment invokes returned cleanup functions, passes `null` to callbacks without cleanup, and clears object refs to `null`. In React 16.8–18, use `null`-based cleanup instead of returning a function.

## Example

### Forwarded and internal refs

A typical use: composing the forwarded ref and an internal ref in a library component.

```tsx
import { forwardRef, useRef } from "react";
import { useComposedRef } from "@lilib/hooks";

const Component = forwardRef<HTMLDivElement, any>((props, ref) => {
  const domRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const composedRef = useComposedRef(domRef, ref);

  // Do something.

  return <div ref={composedRef}>...</div>;
});
```

### Ref cleanup in React 19+

This example combines an object ref with a callback that returns cleanup. It requires React 19+ and a browser with `ResizeObserver` support. When the element detaches, the observer is disconnected and `domRef.current` is cleared to `null`.

```tsx
import { useCallback, useRef, useState } from "react";
import { useComposedRef } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Component() {
  const domRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const [width, setWidth] = useState(0);
  const observeSize = useCallback((node: HTMLDivElement | null) => {
    if (!node) return;

    const observer = new ResizeObserver(([entry]) => {
      setWidth(Math.round(entry.contentRect.width));
    });
    observer.observe(node);

    return () => observer.disconnect();
  }, []);
  const composedRef = useComposedRef(domRef, observeSize);

  return <div ref={composedRef}>Width: {width}px</div>;
}
```

---

# useMountedRef

It returns a ref object that is used to determine whether the component is mounted.

## API

```ts
function useMountedRef(): React.MutableRefObject<boolean>;
```

## Notes

- The flag is set by `useEffect`: during the first render and inside `useLayoutEffect`, `current` is still `false`.
- In StrictMode, the cleanup resets the flag during the simulated unmount.

## Example

The following example loads fake data asynchronously; click Load and unmount the loader before it finishes to see the update being skipped.

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { useMountedRef } from "@lilib/hooks";

// Simulate a slow request that resolves after one second.
function fakeRequest(): Promise<string> {
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    setTimeout(() => resolve("Fake data"), 1000);
  });
}

function Loader({ onSkipped }: { onSkipped: () => void }) {
  const mountedRef = useMountedRef();
  const [result, setResult] = useState("Not loaded");

  async function handleLoad() {
    setResult("Loading...");
    const data = await fakeRequest();
    if (!mountedRef.current) {
      // The component unmounted while loading, skip the state update.
      onSkipped();
      return;
    }
    setResult(data);
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <button onClick={handleLoad}>Load</button> {result}
    </div>
  );
}

function Example() {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(true);
  const [skipped, setSkipped] = useState(0);

  return (
    <>
      <div>
        <button onClick={() => setShow((show) => !show)}>
          {show ? "Unmount" : "Mount"} loader
        </button>
      </div>
      {show && <Loader onSkipped={() => setSkipped((skipped) => skipped + 1)} />}
      <div>Updates skipped after unmount: {skipped}</div>
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

---

# useUnmountedRef

It returns a ref object that is used to determine whether the component is unmounted.

## API

```ts
function useUnmountedRef(): React.MutableRefObject<boolean>;
```

## Notes

- The flag is set by `useEffect`: during the first render and inside `useLayoutEffect`, `current` is still `false`.

## Example

The following example loads fake data asynchronously; click Load and unmount the loader before it finishes to see the update being skipped.

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { useUnmountedRef } from "@lilib/hooks";

// Simulate a slow request that resolves after one second.
function fakeRequest(): Promise<string> {
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    setTimeout(() => resolve("Fake data"), 1000);
  });
}

function Loader({ onSkipped }: { onSkipped: () => void }) {
  const unmountedRef = useUnmountedRef();
  const [result, setResult] = useState("Not loaded");

  async function handleLoad() {
    setResult("Loading...");
    const data = await fakeRequest();
    if (unmountedRef.current) {
      // The component unmounted while loading, skip the state update.
      onSkipped();
      return;
    }
    setResult(data);
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <button onClick={handleLoad}>Load</button> {result}
    </div>
  );
}

function Example() {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(true);
  const [skipped, setSkipped] = useState(0);

  return (
    <>
      <div>
        <button onClick={() => setShow((show) => !show)}>
          {show ? "Unmount" : "Mount"} loader
        </button>
      </div>
      {show && <Loader onSkipped={() => setSkipped((skipped) => skipped + 1)} />}
      <div>Updates skipped after unmount: {skipped}</div>
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

---

# useTitle

Set the document title.

## API

```ts
function useTitle(title: string | null, options?: { restore?: boolean }): void;
```

Parameters:

- **`title`:** The document title. Pass `null` to not set one.
- **`options`:** Options object.
  - **`options.restore`:** Whether to restore the previous title on unmount.

## Notes

- With `restore`, the original title is captured on the hook's first render; when several components restore, the last one to unmount wins.

## Example

The following example syncs the browser tab title with the input.

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { useTitle } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const [title, setTitle] = useState("");
  useTitle(title, { restore: true });

  return (
    <input
      placeholder="Enter title"
      value={title}
      onChange={(event) => {
        setTitle(event.target.value);
      }}
    />
  );
}

export default Example;
```

---

# useFavicon

Set the document favicon.

## API

```ts
function useFavicon(href: string | null, options?: { mime?: string; restore?: boolean }): void;
```

Parameters:

- **`href`:** The favicon URL. Pass `null` to not set one.
- **`options`:** Options object.
  - **`options.mime`:** Specify the MIME type. It is inferred from the `href` extname by default (support `.png`, `.gif`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.svg`, `.webp` and `.ico`).
  - **`options.restore`:** Whether to restore the previous favicon on unmount.

## Notes

- The first `link[rel*='icon']` element in `<head>` is reused (which may be an `apple-touch-icon` or similar); a new link is created only when none exists.
- With `restore`, the original favicon is captured on the hook's first render; multiple instances will override each other.

## Example

The following example switches the favicon together with the title when the brand changes.

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { useFavicon, useTitle } from "@lilib/hooks";

const brands = {
  lilib: { title: "Lilib", icon: "https://lilib.dev/favicon.ico" },
  react: { title: "React", icon: "https://react.dev/favicon.ico" },
};

function Example() {
  const [brand, setBrand] = useState<keyof typeof brands>("lilib");
  const meta = brands[brand];

  useTitle(meta.title);
  useFavicon(meta.icon, { restore: true });

  return (
    <select
      value={brand}
      onChange={(event) => {
        setBrand(event.target.value as keyof typeof brands);
      }}
    >
      <option value="lilib">Lilib</option>
      <option value="react">React</option>
    </select>
  );
}
```

# useOnline

Detect whether the network is online. In a non-browser environment, it always returns `true`.

## API

```ts
function useOnline(): boolean;
```

Results:

- Returns `true` if the network is online, otherwise `false`.

## Notes

- `navigator.onLine` only reports whether the device is connected to a network (e.g. a router); it does not guarantee internet access.

## Example

The following example shows a banner when the network goes offline.

```tsx
import { useOnline } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const online = useOnline();

  return (
    <div style={{ padding: 8, backgroundColor: online ? "#d4edda" : "#f8d7da" }}>
      {online ? "The network is online" : "You are offline"}
    </div>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

# useDarkMode

Detect whether the preferred color scheme of the system is dark.

## API

```ts
function useDarkMode(): boolean;
```

Results:

- Returns `true` if the system prefers dark mode, otherwise `false`.

## Notes

- This hook is read-only: it reflects the system preference and cannot be toggled programmatically. To implement a user-overridable theme, manage the state yourself (e.g. with `useLocalStorage`).
- Returns `false` in non-browser environments and in browsers without `prefers-color-scheme` support.

## Example

The following example switches a card between light and dark themes based on the system preference.

```tsx
import { useDarkMode } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const isDarkMode = useDarkMode();

  return (
    <div
      style={{
        padding: 16,
        border: "1px solid rgba(128, 128, 128, 0.25)",
        color: isDarkMode ? "#ffffff" : "#000000",
        backgroundColor: isDarkMode ? "#1b1b1d" : "#f5f6f7",
      }}
    >
      {isDarkMode ? "Dark theme" : "Light theme"} (prefers-color-scheme:{" "}
      {isDarkMode ? "dark" : "light"})
    </div>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

# usePageVisible

Detect whether the page is visible. The `visibilitychange` event doesn't fire when restoring from the bfcache, so this hook also listens to the `pageshow` event to re-detect.

## API

```ts
function usePageVisible(): boolean;
```

Results:

- Returns `true` if the page is visible, otherwise `false`.

## Notes

- Returns `true` in non-browser environments.

## Example

The following example pauses a timer while the page is hidden (typical for pausing video).

```tsx
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";
import { usePageVisible } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const visible = usePageVisible();
  const [elapsed, setElapsed] = useState(0);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!visible) {
      // Pause while the page is hidden.
      return;
    }
    const timer = setInterval(() => {
      setElapsed((elapsed) => elapsed + 1);
    }, 1000);
    return () => clearInterval(timer);
  }, [visible]);

  return (
    <div>
      <div>The page is {visible ? "visible" : "hidden"}.</div>
      <div>Elapsed seconds (pauses while hidden): {elapsed}</div>
    </div>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

```ts
function useWindowFocus(): boolean;
```

- Returns `true` if the `window` has focus, otherwise `false`.

## Notes

- `document.hasFocus()` also returns `true` when a nested iframe has focus.

The following example shows a notice when the window loses focus.

```tsx
import { useWindowFocus } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {

  return (
    <div style={{ padding: 8, backgroundColor: focus ? "#d4edda" : "#fff3cd" }}>
      {focus ? "The window has focus" : "The window lost focus"}
    </div>

export default Example;
```

# useMatchMedia

Use [`window.matchMedia()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/matchMedia) to determine whether the document matches the media query string.

## API

```ts
function useMatchMedia(query: string, defaultValue?: boolean): boolean;
```

Parameters:

- **`query`:** The media query string.
- **`defaultValue`:** The default return value in non-browser environments. Default is `false`.

Results:

- Returns `true` if the document matches the query, otherwise `false`.

## Notes

- `defaultValue` only applies in non-browser environments; on the client the result comes from `window.matchMedia`. Mind hydration mismatches when the default differs from the client result.
- Prefer CSS media queries for style-only changes; use this hook when JavaScript logic depends on the match.

## Example

The following example switches the layout when the viewport is narrower than 600px.

```tsx
import { useMatchMedia } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const isNarrow = useMatchMedia("(max-width: 600px)");

  return (
    <div style={{ display: "flex", flexDirection: isNarrow ? "column" : "row", gap: 8 }}>
      <div style={{ flex: 1, padding: 16, backgroundColor: "rgba(255, 165, 0, 0.4)" }}>Sidebar</div>
      <div style={{ flex: 2, padding: 16, backgroundColor: "rgba(0, 128, 255, 0.4)" }}>Content</div>
    </div>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

# useWindowSize

Get the window size.

## API

```ts
function useWindowSize(): {
  width: number | undefined;
  height: number | undefined;
};
```

Results:

- **`width`:** Window width, or `undefined` outside the browser.
- **`height`:** Window height, or `undefined` outside the browser.

## Notes

- The size comes from `window.innerWidth`/`innerHeight`, which include scrollbars.
- On mobile, collapsing or expanding the address bar changes the viewport without firing a window `resize`; the hook also listens to `visualViewport.resize` for that.

## Example

The following example switches the layout based on the window width; resize the browser window to see the effect.

```tsx
import { useWindowSize } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const { width = 0 } = useWindowSize();

  return (
    <>
      <div>Window width: {width}px</div>
      <div style={{ display: "flex", flexDirection: width < 600 ? "column" : "row", gap: 8 }}>
        <div style={{ flex: 1, padding: 16, backgroundColor: "rgba(255, 165, 0, 0.4)" }}>
          Sidebar
        </div>
        <div style={{ flex: 2, padding: 16, backgroundColor: "rgba(0, 128, 255, 0.4)" }}>
          Content
        </div>
      </div>
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```

# useElementSize

Get the size of a DOM element.

## API

```ts
function useElementSize(target: Element | React.RefObject<Element | null>): {
  width: number | undefined;
  height: number | undefined;
};
```

Parameters:

- **`target`:** A DOM element, or a ref object that references a DOM element.

Results:

- **`width`:** Element width, or `undefined` when the target is invalid.
- **`height`:** Element height, or `undefined` when the target is invalid.

## Notes

- The size comes from `getBoundingClientRect`: it includes padding and border, excludes margin, is affected by transforms, and may be fractional.
- Both values are `undefined` until the target element is mounted.

## Example

The following example shows the element size; click Toggle size to see it change.

```tsx
import { useRef, useState } from "react";
import { useElementSize } from "@lilib/hooks";

function Example() {
  const [wide, setWide] = useState(false);
  const ref = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const { width = 0, height = 0 } = useElementSize(ref);

  return (
    <>
      <div>
        <button onClick={() => setWide((wide) => !wide)}>Toggle size</button>
      </div>
      <div
        ref={ref}
        style={{
          padding: 16,
          width: wide ? "100%" : "50%",
          border: "1px solid rgba(128, 128, 128, 0.25)",
        }}
      >
        Element size: {JSON.stringify({ width, height })}
      </div>
    </>
  );
}

export default Example;
```
